problem: Monolithic embodied policies entangle heterogeneous capabilities (perception, planning, control) in one parameter set, causing opaque coupling, capability isolation and entangled optimization. Tool-based embodied work is fragmented, with no standard protocol, no validated tool suite, and no systematic evaluation of tool use.
motivation: Embodied decision-making is hierarchical and heterogeneous, so externalizing capabilities as independently optimized, callable tools could allow reuse, diagnosis and composition across models. It is unclear whether current models can reliably use such tools, and which capabilities benefit from externalization.
key_idea: Externalize embodied capabilities as independently optimized tools behind a standardized Embodied Tool Protocol (ETP) with 100+ validated tools, and evaluate tool-use competence with EmbodiedToolBench.
insight: Tool augmentation gives large gains for perception and cognition (e.g. EB-ALFRED +0.31, EB-Navigation +0.36; Qwen3-8B 0.20 to 0.72) but small gains for execution/low-level control (EB-Manipulation +0.07, Long-horizon +0.01). The bottleneck is tool competence rather than availability: models miss tool invocations (recall as low as 0.31), pick wrong tools (CSR at most 0.74), ignore returned outputs (AMR is low), and over-compose tool chains.
method: Embodied Tool Protocol (ETP): each tool is a callable unit with a declared interface (X_m, Y_m), a capability subset and an executable mapping, which can be a learned model, an algorithm or a program.

Registry-based discovery and invocation: a registry stores capability descriptions and schema constraints; the agent selects tools by declared functionality and builds schema-conforming queries, so new tools can be added without changing the agent policy.
Isolated execution: each call runs in an isolated session that returns output and runtime feedback, supporting concurrent and remote execution.

Tool suite: 100+ SOTA methods across four capability dimensions (Perception and Grounding, Cognition and State Modeling, Reasoning and Planning, Execution and Control), each wrapped as an API with an LLM-generated tool card.
EmbodiedToolBench: four tasks (tool-need recognition, tool selection, tool execution in two stages, tool-chain composition), 100 samples each across 4 embodied environments.

Tool-augmented decision process: the agent picks a tool or none, queries it, and conditions its action on the output; this is a bi-level formulation with independently trained tools and an orchestrating policy.

setting.backbone: Frozen MLLMs used as orchestrators: GPT-4o, GPT-5-chat, Claude-3.7, Claude-4.6, Qwen3-VL-32B/8B, Qwen2.5-VL-32B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B; tools are pretrained SOTA models
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB images plus text instructions (EmbodiedBench), real-world camera
setting.action_space: EmbodiedBench high-level actions (EB-ALFRED/Habitat skills, EB-Navigation discrete moves, EB-Manipulation arm actions) plus tool calls
setting.simulator: EmbodiedBench (ALFRED/AI2-THOR, Habitat, EB-Navigation, EB-Manipulation) and real world

results: Tool augmentation raises average success by 0.31 on EB-ALFRED and 0.36 on EB-Navigation, but only 0.14 on EB-Habitat and 0.07 on EB-Manipulation. Qwen3-8B with tools (0.72) beats GPT-4o without tools (0.48) on EB-ALFRED. In real-world tasks all models score 0/10 without tools and 4-9/10 with tools.
limitations: Gains are limited for execution, contact-rich and long-horizon tasks, and tool calls add latency (over 30s on EB-Manipulation).
Models still fail at tool-need recognition, selection, output utilization and over-composition, with tool-induced bias in errors.
Evaluation is on EmbodiedBench-style high-level tasks with small samples (100 per benchmark task) and no navigation benchmark like R2R.
compares_to: Tool-free MLLM baselines (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Claude-3.7, Claude-4.6, Qwen family)
